paragraphs: The paper asks how reinforcement can change the way sensory cortex represents incoming information. Its motivation comes from adult animals: substantial changes in sensory representations can follow tasks that pair stimuli with reinforcement, or experiments that pair sensory input with stimulation of neuromodulatory nuclei. Presenting sensory stimuli alone usually does not produce the same effect.

This creates a gap between two traditions of learning theory. Unsupervised accounts explain how representations can develop from sensory experience, but tend to leave reinforcement out of adult plasticity. Reinforcement learning, meanwhile, has generally concentrated on choosing actions in uncertain environments, rather than explaining how sensory representations change alongside action learning.

The authors develop a framework that adds reinforcement effects to generative-model accounts of cortical encoding in a biologically plausible way. Its contribution is to connect learning what sensory inputs represent with learning what is behaviorally consequential. The abstract presents this framework as an extension of existing representational accounts, without claiming that unsupervised learning has no role in development or evolution.
neurips-2003-a-biologically-plausible-al.tldr: The paper develops a biologically plausible framework for incorporating reinforcement into the learning of sensory representations.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to classify multimedia sequences whose lengths can vary. Its central idea is to describe the data with probabilistic models and then compare those models inside a support vector machine. This connects a generative description of the observations with a discriminative method for separating classes.

The authors derive a kernel distance using Kullback–Leibler divergence between generative models. They explore Gaussian mixtures and single Gaussian models with full covariance for speech and image applications. The resulting kernels replace standard SVM kernels and provide an alternative to the Fisher kernel. Comparing probabilistic descriptions gives the classifier a way to work with sequence data without requiring all sequences to have the same length.

Experiments cover speaker verification, speaker identification, and image classification. The proposed kernels achieve the best speaker-verification performance among the evaluated methods. For identification and image classification, they mostly outperform Fisher-kernel SVMs and generative classifiers. That distinction matters: the reported advantage is broad across the experiments, but is not described as an improvement in every comparison.
neurips-2003-a-kullback-leibler-divergen.tldr: Kernels built from KL divergence between probabilistic models improve several reported speech and image classification comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper learns a connection between image content and descriptive words so that a system can automatically annotate pictures and retrieve them using text. It starts from images that already have annotations, using these examples to learn how visual features and words occur together.

The method assumes that each image has been divided into regions, with each region represented by a vector of continuous numerical features. The authors build a joint probabilistic model of those features and the annotation words. Given an image's regions, the model can then estimate the probability of generating a particular word. This makes the connection between visual evidence and language explicit within one probabilistic framework.

The same learned relationship supports both applications: proposing words for an image and finding images relevant to a query word. Experiments show significant improvements over the best previously reported results on annotation and retrieval. These findings support the usefulness of jointly modeling image regions and words for both tasks under the paper's region-based representation.
neurips-2003-a-model-for-learning-the-se.tldr: A joint probabilistic model of image regions and words improves automatic image annotation and text-based image retrieval.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much information about a visual scene can be recovered from the activity of V1 neurons in awake monkeys. Decoding turns recorded neural responses into an estimate of a scene variable, making it possible to assess what those responses reveal about the visual input.

The authors develop a parametric Bayesian decoder that updates its estimates sequentially using particle filtering. Its distinguishing feature is the use of Volterra kernels to filter particles in a high-dimensional space. The method therefore combines sequential probabilistic estimation with the specified relationship between the visual signal and neural activity. In the reported comparisons, it consistently performs better than the optimal linear decoder.

The results suggest that real-time decoding of a critical variable could require as few as ten independent, similar neurons for a particular class of stimuli. This is a conditional finding about that setting. The reconstructed variable also predicts neural activity about as well as the actual signal when assessed through the Volterra kernels, supporting the reconstruction's relevance to the modeled neural responses.
neurips-2003-decoding-v1-neuronal-activi.tldr: A Bayesian particle-filter decoder outperforms an optimal linear decoder and suggests that a small population of similar, independent V1 neurons could support real-time decoding.

paragraphs: The paper develops a protocol for improving the dynamic behavior of networks made from simple electronic devices. Examples include sensor networks, mobile-device networks, and communication switches. The practical challenge is to improve the network's overall performance using only local communication and modest computation at individual devices.

The approach extends policy-gradient methods for Markov decision processes to a team of agents. Devices communicate and compute asynchronously while contributing to an aggregate performance objective. A motivating sensor-network problem involves power consumption, delay, and buffer overflow, illustrating why local choices must be coordinated around consequences for the network as a whole.

The authors establish that the protocol's dynamics approximate an ordinary differential equation that follows the gradient of the performance objective. This provides a mathematical connection between the distributed updates and the desired optimization direction. Together with the protocol's stated scalability, the result explains how simple local operations can support optimization in large networks without requiring every device to perform a centralized computation.
neurips-2003-distributed-optimization-in.tldr: A scalable protocol uses local, asynchronous device updates to approximate policy-gradient optimization of overall network performance.

paragraphs: The paper compares human curve detection with an ideal observer built from the probability model that generates the curves. This creates a reference tied to the structure of the task: human performance can be assessed against an observer that uses the specified statistical information about the targets.

The generative model describes both curve geometry and local image intensity. The ideal observer applies Bayesian inference with maximum a posteriori estimation. By changing the probability model for geometry, the authors test whether people detect some kinds of curves relatively better than others, especially curves with shape statistics resembling those found in nature. Experiments use both rectangular and hexagonal lattices.

Human performance approaches that of the ideal observer and is generally closest when target curves tend to be straight or follow natural curve statistics. The result suggests a human perceptual bias toward these shapes. Comparing against the corresponding ideal observer helps relate that preference to the statistical detection task, rather than treating performance on each curve family in isolation.
neurips-2003-human-and-ideal-observers-f.tldr: Human curve detection approaches an ideal observer most closely for straight curves and curves with natural shape statistics.

paragraphs: The paper addresses inference of an entire hidden state sequence in a nonlinear dynamical system from observed data. It introduces a Markov chain sampling method that updates all times together, allowing a proposed trajectory to be selected as a connected sequence rather than as separate state choices.

Each update first creates a pool of candidate states at every time. The authors then construct an embedded hidden Markov model whose state labels identify entries in those pools. A forward-backward dynamic programming procedure selects a sequence with the appropriate probabilities. This avoids explicitly enumerating the exponentially many trajectories that can be formed by combining pool entries across time.

The method is illustrated with a one-dimensional example and another example showing how the embedded model can effectively discretize the state space without introducing discretization error. A larger application compares it with a particle smoother for recovering human motion from two-dimensional marker traces. These examples connect the sequence-sampling construction to both its handling of continuous states and a substantial motion-inference task.
neurips-2003-inferring-state-sequences-f.tldr: An embedded hidden Markov model efficiently samples whole hidden trajectories from pools of candidate states in nonlinear systems.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how information evolves within recurrent networks of spiking neurons. It examines generic cortical microcircuit models, whose internal states are high-dimensional, to ask what computations such circuits can perform on complex patterns of arriving spikes.

The authors use Bayesian and linear classifiers as an efficient way to analyze information in those states. This shifts the analysis toward what can be extracted from the network's activity as it changes. The relevant information includes the order in which spikes arrive and context acquired previously, so the question concerns both incoming events and the circuit's preceding experience.

The study shows that these modeled recurrent circuits have an inherent capacity for rapid computation that merges spike-order information with earlier context. The significance is that a circuit's current response can reflect the temporal organization of new input together with information already present in its state. The stated finding concerns the computational capabilities of the microcircuit models, linking recurrent spiking dynamics to contextual processing.
neurips-2003-information-dynamics-and-em.tldr: Analysis of recurrent spiking microcircuit models shows rapid computations that combine spike arrival order with previously acquired context.

paragraphs: The paper extends approximate linear programming to decision problems with continuous states. The starting point is its use for complex factored Markov decision processes with finite state spaces. The authors ask whether the same general optimization approach can also work when a state consists of multiple continuously varying factors.

They show how to construct an approximate linear-programming solution for a factored continuous-state model and contrast it with existing solution methods. The factored description matters because the target problems have many state components. The contribution is therefore an explicit extension of the approximation approach to a setting beyond the finite-state problems that motivated it.

Experiments examine three continuous-state decision problems with 24 to 25 state factors. These results support the authors' argument that the method offers a robust alternative for high-dimensional continuous-state problems. The finding establishes successful applications of the approach in the studied settings, giving a concrete basis for considering approximate linear programming when the state cannot be represented as a finite collection of possibilities.
neurips-2003-linear-program-approximatio.tldr: Approximate linear programming is extended successfully to factored continuous-state decision problems with 24–25 state factors.

paragraphs: Belief propagation provides an efficient way to approximate probabilities in graphs containing cycles. The paper starts from its estimates for individual nodes and neighboring pairs, then addresses a broader question: how to estimate joint probabilities for any pair of nodes, including nodes that are not directly connected.

The authors propose two algorithms for this purpose. One uses propagation, while the other uses matrix inversion. Both aim to recover information about pairs that goes beyond knowing each node's probability separately. Joint probabilities matter because they describe how two variables behave together, which individual-node estimates alone do not determine.

The paper proves several desirable properties of the resulting estimates. For the propagation algorithm, it establishes convergence when belief propagation converges to a stable fixed point. This is a conditional guarantee tied to the behavior of the underlying belief-propagation procedure. Experiments compare competing methods, complementing the theoretical analysis with an empirical examination of approaches to arbitrary-pair inference.
neurips-2003-linear-response-for-approxi.tldr: Two algorithms extend approximate inference to arbitrary node pairs, with a conditional convergence guarantee for the propagation-based method.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict whether two entities are linked and what kind of link connects them. In relational data, these decisions occur within a larger network of objects and relationships. The authors therefore model link predictions jointly with entity attributes and the rest of the link graph.

Their approach uses relational Markov networks and defines probabilistic patterns over subgraph structures. These patterns allow the model to represent relationships among link labels, rather than treating each possible link as an isolated classification problem. Collective classification makes the surrounding relational structure part of the prediction process.

The method is applied to two datasets: university webpages and a social network. The reported results show significant accuracy improvements over flat classification, which predicts links independently. The findings support both the use of collective prediction and the inclusion of subgraph patterns over link labels. They show that, in these applications, modeling how relationships fit together supplies useful predictive information beyond a separate decision for each link.
neurips-2003-link-prediction-in-relation.tldr: Joint relational models using subgraph patterns improve link prediction over independent classification on webpage and social-network data.

paragraphs: The paper examines when minimizing a regularized classification loss leads toward a separator with maximum margin. Margin provides a geometric view of a classifier's separation of classes and helps support analysis of generalization error. The authors seek a shared explanation for this behavior across several widely used losses.

They formulate and prove a sufficient condition under which solutions approach margin-maximizing separators as regularization vanishes. The condition covers the hinge loss used in support vector machines, the exponential loss associated with AdaBoost, and logistic regression loss. This places these different objectives within a common account of their limiting geometric behavior.

The result is specifically about convergence as regularization becomes arbitrarily small, and the condition is sufficient rather than asserted to be necessary. The authors also extend the analysis to multiclass classification and present margin-maximizing multiclass versions of logistic regression and support vector machines. The contribution thus combines a unifying theoretical condition with corresponding classifier formulations for problems involving more than two classes.
neurips-2003-margin-maximizing-loss-func.tldr: A sufficient condition explains when regularized classification losses approach maximum-margin solutions as regularization vanishes.

paragraphs: Mutual Boosting aims to improve object detection by allowing detectors to use contextual information from related objects and parts. The paper's example involves eyes, noses, mouths, and faces, where evidence for individual components and evidence for the whole object can inform one another.

The method trains multiple detectors in parallel using AdaBoost. During training, a detector can use the other intermediate detectors to expand its available set of weak learners. This generalizes the efficient features associated with Viola and Jones and enables information to pass between parts and objects in a compositional hierarchy. Context becomes part of the detector's learned evidence.

Experiments train the facial-part and face detectors within this framework. The reported results outperform applications that overlook contextual information, supporting the value of exchanging information among related detection tasks. The authors suggest that contextual integration is a step toward human-like detection capabilities. That broader interpretation accompanies the demonstrated improvement, rather than establishing that the system matches human detection.
neurips-2003-mutual-boosting-for-context.tldr: Mutual Boosting improves detection by letting jointly trained object and part detectors use one another as contextual evidence.

paragraphs: The paper examines AdaBoost as a dynamical system to understand how its repeated updates affect classification margins. The authors derive a simplified nonlinear iterated map and study low-dimensional cases. In these cases, they find stable cycles that can be used to solve explicitly for AdaBoost's output.

This analysis proves a conjecture that AdaBoost may fail to converge to a maximum-margin combined classifier when its weak learning algorithm is non-optimal. The conclusion identifies a possible failure under that condition; it does not say that AdaBoost always fails to maximize margins. Viewing the updates as a dynamical process makes this behavior accessible to direct mathematical analysis.

The authors also investigate how coordinate-based optimization could explicitly target maximum margin. Although AdaBoost is a coordinate-descent method, the cited margin-focused alternatives do not share that characterization. They identify a differentiable function whose coordinate ascent yields a maximum-margin solution, then approximate it to derive a new boosting algorithm with updates slightly more aggressive than those of arc-gv.
neurips-2003-on-the-dynamics-of-boosting.tldr: A dynamical analysis proves that AdaBoost can miss maximum margin with a non-optimal weak learner and motivates a new boosting algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the memory and computation costs of online classification with kernels. In this setting, predictions can depend on many previously seen examples. Keeping and using a large history can make an otherwise incremental learning procedure expensive, motivating a way to reduce the examples retained for prediction.

The authors describe and analyze a simple method that performs this reduction while learning proceeds. Its focus is the number of past examples used by the classifier, connecting resource control directly to the representation used for future predictions. The approach is designed to make that reduction on the fly as training examples are processed.

Experiments on real datasets show that the proposed approach is competitive with a support vector machine after just one pass through the training data. The compared SVM is a batch method that accesses each example multiple times. The result supports the practical value of reducing the retained history during online learning while achieving competitive classification performance in the reported experiments.
neurips-2003-online-classification-on-a-.tldr: An online method reduces the past examples needed for kernel prediction and remains competitive with an SVM after one training pass.

paragraphs: The paper connects clustering from pairwise similarities to probabilistic graphical models. Pairwise methods, including spectral clustering, can separate clusters with complex shapes. However, the authors note that spectral methods lack a straightforward probabilistic interpretation, which makes it difficult to learn their parameters automatically from training data.

Using the previously proposed typical-cut framework, they establish an equivalence between computing a typical cut and performing inference in an undirected graphical model. This connection makes probabilistic inference methods available for the clustering problem. The authors show that exact inference may remain possible for some problems containing hundreds of data points.

For more complicated datasets, loopy belief propagation and generalized belief propagation produce excellent results on challenging clustering problems. The graphical-model formulation also leads to an algorithm for learning affinity matrices from labeled data. The contribution therefore goes beyond a reinterpretation: the connection supplies ways to compute clusterings and to learn the pairwise similarities on which those clusterings depend.
neurips-2003-pairwise-clustering-and-gra.tldr: An equivalence between typical-cut clustering and graphical-model inference enables probabilistic clustering methods and learned affinity matrices.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether an algorithm connected to an unfamiliar body can discover properties of that body and its environment. It considers questions such as recognizing that the world is three-dimensional and finding how to move in a straight line, despite having access only to high-dimensional sensory inputs and motor outputs.

The proposed route is to analyze the relationship between motor commands and their sensory consequences. The authors show that this relationship can reveal information about the world's structure regardless of the particular devices making up the body. This makes the connection between action and perception the basis for discovering physical organization.

Simulation results demonstrate a way to issue motor commands that produce fundamental bodily movements relative to the structure of the physical world. The contribution is a positive demonstration that meaningful spatial information and movement can be derived through sensory-motor relationships. It gives substance to the initial questions by showing how an algorithm can approach them without starting from a known description of its sensors and effectors.
neurips-2003-perception-of-the-structure.tldr: An algorithm can infer physical structure and generate fundamental movements by analyzing how motor outputs affect unfamiliar sensory inputs.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to turn comparisons between pairs of classes into probabilities for a multiclass problem. Pairwise coupling starts with all class-pair comparisons and combines their information. The desired output is a probability for each class, providing more information than simply naming a winning class.

The authors propose two approaches to obtaining those probabilities. Both can be reduced to solving linear systems, and both are described as easy to implement. This gives the combination step a concrete computational form: evidence from the separate pairwise comparisons is brought together through a system of equations.

The paper supports the proposed methods with both conceptual analysis and experiments. The authors report greater stability than two popular existing approaches, including voting. The stated advantage concerns the stability of the resulting methods, which is relevant when combining many separate comparisons into one set of class probabilities. The contribution is therefore a pair of practical probability-estimation procedures with analytical and empirical support for their stability.
neurips-2003-probability-estimates-for-m.tldr: Two easily implemented linear-system methods produce multiclass probabilities from pairwise comparisons with improved reported stability.

paragraphs: The paper studies probability forecasts whose stated probabilities agree with observed frequencies. It introduces a finite-sample formalization of this calibration requirement and analyzes it under the assumption that object-label pairs are independent and identically distributed. The task is to forecast possible labels for a new object using training examples.

Under the proposed definition, no ordinary probability-forecasting algorithm is automatically calibrated. The authors instead allow a forecast to be a set of probability measures, ideally a narrow set. They identify a broad class of such multiprobability algorithms that satisfies the calibration property and call them Venn probability machines. Allowing a set changes what the forecasting procedure can guarantee.

Experiments show that a Venn machine based on one-nearest-neighbor performs reasonably well on a standard benchmark. A separate theoretical result establishes that a simple Venn machine approaches the true conditional probabilities asymptotically, without knowing the generating distribution. Within the stated randomness setting, the paper thus combines a finite-sample calibration framework with a long-run probability-estimation result.
neurips-2003-self-calibrating-probabilit.tldr: Under independent, identically distributed sampling, Venn probability machines achieve a finite-sample calibration property by outputting sets of probability measures.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent amino-acid sequences for protein classification when unlabeled sequences are much more plentiful than labeled examples. Here, labeled proteins have known three-dimensional structures and belong to structural classes. The authors build on strong classification results from string kernels while seeking to use the additional unlabeled data.

They develop simple, scalable cluster-kernel techniques that incorporate unlabeled sequences into the representation. This places the extra data inside the way proteins are compared for classification. The approach makes the abundance of unlabeled sequences useful for a supervised task whose structural labels are relatively scarce.

The reported methods substantially improve string-kernel classification performance and outperform standard ways of using unlabeled data, including adding close homologs of positive examples to training. They also match or exceed previously presented cluster-kernel methods while requiring much less computation. The results support both parts of the contribution: unlabeled data improves the representation, and the proposed techniques provide that benefit with greater computational efficiency than earlier cluster-kernel approaches.
neurips-2003-semi-supervised-protein-cla.tldr: Scalable cluster kernels use unlabeled protein sequences to improve classification while greatly reducing computation relative to earlier cluster-kernel methods.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an automated debugging strategy based on sampled information from thousands of actual user executions. Its goal is to identify program features most strongly associated with crashes. This makes evidence from many real runs the starting point for deciding where debugging attention should be directed.

The authors formulate that search as maximizing a defined utility function. The function provides a quantitative way to choose features that are informative about failures, and the approach has connections to intuitive debugging heuristics. The central move is to express the search for useful debugging clues as an optimization problem over collected execution data.

Demonstrations show that the strategy can handle several types of bugs occurring in real programs. The findings support using statistical patterns across many sampled runs to help pinpoint relevant features. Because the stated target is correlation with crashes, the selected features serve as evidence for debugging; the abstract's claim is about finding useful crash-associated clues rather than automatically proving the causal explanation of every failure.
neurips-2003-statistical-debugging-of-sa.tldr: A utility-maximizing method uses sampled user executions to identify program features associated with crashes.

paragraphs: The paper reports learning experiments with silicon spiking neurons whose synapses change according to spike timing. The aim is to examine how this hardware responds to temporal correlations in its inputs and whether it can learn to detect synchrony across spike trains.

The synaptic update scheme supports two modes: weight-independent and weight-dependent changes. The authors characterize the implemented learning window in each mode, describing how the timing relationship between spikes affects learning. When the neurons receive spike trains with different types of synchronization, their synaptic weights develop bimodal distributions, with weights concentrated around two modes.

The authors also demonstrate hierarchical synchrony detection in a two-layer network of these silicon neurons. This extends the evidence from synaptic learning behavior to a network-level computation performed across layers. Together, the results connect the measured timing-dependent learning mechanism, the weight distributions it produces, and the ability of a small hardware network to detect temporal structure hierarchically.
neurips-2003-synchrony-detection-by-anal.tldr: Silicon neurons with timing-dependent synapses develop bimodal weights and demonstrate hierarchical synchrony detection in a two-layer network.

paragraphs: The paper treats a biochemical relay between cells as a communication channel. A sending cell releases a diffusible ligand, and a receiving cell detects it through binding to a receptor in its membrane. The authors use this simplified setting to investigate how much information such a relay can transmit.

The receptor-ligand interaction produces a nonlinear channel with noise that is not Gaussian. The authors model the channel numerically and examine how it responds to input signals at different frequencies. Randomness enters through both ligand diffusion and receptor binding, so the analysis includes fluctuations in signal transport as well as reception.

These stochastic effects give the channel low-pass characteristics, meaning that its response favors slower variations over faster ones. The authors estimate channel capacity using a water-filling formula adapted from the additive white Gaussian noise setting. The result connects the physical behavior of diffusion and binding to an information-processing description, while retaining the paper's framing of capacity as an estimate for a simplified biochemical relay.
neurips-2003-the-diffusion-limited-bioch.tldr: A numerical model links diffusion and receptor-binding noise to low-pass behavior and an estimated capacity for biochemical signaling.

paragraphs: The paper asks when non-negative matrix factorization can recover the actual parts that generated data. It gives the problem a geometric interpretation: find a simplicial cone that encloses the observed points while remaining inside the region where every coordinate is non-negative.

The authors show that this cone is unique under certain conditions, broadly requiring data to spread across faces of that non-negative region. They construct synthetic image-articulation databases satisfying the conditions through separated support and factorial sampling. For these databases, a generative description in terms of parts exists, and NMF correctly identifies those parts.

The conditions matter because the recovery claim is tied to how the data occupy the space and how the examples are generated. The authors test published NMF algorithms on one of their synthetic databases and find that their theoretical results predict the algorithms' performance. The contribution connects geometric uniqueness, a specific parts-based generative setting, and observed behavior of existing implementations.
neurips-2003-when-does-non-negative-matr.tldr: Geometric conditions establish when NMF uniquely recovers generating parts, with supporting results on synthetic image data.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a weakness of learning energy-based probability models using short Markov chain simulations. Starting a chain at the data and running it for only a few steps can work well, but separated concentrations of data create a particular difficulty for these brief sampling runs.

When regions of high probability are divided by very low-density regions, a short chain cannot readily move between them. As a result, learning may fail to establish the correct relative energies of different modes. The issue concerns how much probability the model assigns to separate regions, which cannot be reliably compared if sampled particles remain within their starting mode.

The authors improve brief sampling by introducing long-range moves suggested by the data distribution. These moves provide a route between otherwise separated modes. They state that such proposals have a reasonable acceptance rate when the model is approximately correct. The method therefore addresses the specific obstacle of crossing low-density gaps, with its acceptance claim explicitly depending on the quality of the current model.
neurips-2003-wormholes-improve-contrasti.tldr: Data-guided long-range sampling moves help short Markov chains connect separated modes during energy-based model learning.
